title: Network permission, release signing, component library and the offline test for US-01-01

question:
How should US-01-01 handle the network permission, release signing, the component library and the offline test? I propose the four points below as they stand.

Done on feature/US-01-01 (WIP 4462e0c): minSdk 31, the TC-01-01 Maestro flow, and the platform versions in README.md. The rest needs your call.

The debug build that yarn stack and CI test loads its JavaScript from Metro over a local socket, and Android refuses that without INTERNET. TC-01-02 steps 2 and 3 expect the category screen and a card. Those arrive with US-02-01 and US-03-01, so that test case cannot pass in this story.

- Network: INTERNET is removed from the release build only, through a release manifest written by a config plugin; the debug build keeps it for Metro. Criterion 3 is proven by a unit test on that manifest and by aapt on a built release APK.
- Signing: the release build reads the keystore path, alias and passwords from Gradle properties KQ_UPLOAD_* in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties or the environment. Without them it fails instead of signing with the debug key.
- Component library: none. React Native core components with the app's own black and white theme tokens, written into constitution.md Stack (DEC-07 allows none).
- Offline test: criterion 4 is proven now by a derived test AC-01-01-4 (airplane mode on, the app opens its first screen). The TC-01-02 flow is written once the category screen and cards exist (US-03-01).

a) Take all four points as proposed — yarn stack and CI stay on the debug build. The shipped APK has no network permission, checked by a unit test and on the release APK. TC-01-02 runs from US-03-01; until then criterion 4 rests on the derived test. (recommended)
b) As a, but no INTERNET in any build and e2e on the release build — The tested app is exactly the shipped one. But yarn stack and the acceptance script switch to a release build with the bundle embedded: no Metro or live reload, longer CI builds, and the foundation's start command changes.
c) As a, but leave the component library to US-02-01 — The first real screen chooses it with its design in view. constitution.md Stack stays open until then, and this story makes no UI choice.

Why a: It meets NFR-05 for the APK that reaches the Kompakt without changing the foundation's start command or CI. It adds no dependency and leaves every reviewed test case untouched.

title: Upload key variables in the environment win over Gradle properties of the same name

question:
When a KQ_UPLOAD_* signing value is set both in the environment and in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties, should the environment win?

Review found that the acceptance run passes a throwaway key through KQ_UPLOAD_* environment variables, but the build read gradle.properties first. On your machine, where the real upload key sits in gradle.properties as the README says, the test build was signed with the real key and the signature check failed.

DEC-44 allows both sources but does not say which wins. Your normal release build, with values only in gradle.properties, is unchanged under either option.

a) Environment wins over gradle.properties (implemented) — A key passed in for one build, like the acceptance run's throwaway key, is always used and your real key is never touched by tests. Unit-tested and documented in the README. Cost: a stray KQ_UPLOAD_* exported in your shell would override your real key for a release build. (recommended)
b) gradle.properties wins; tests pass the throwaway with -P — Keeps the old precedence. The acceptance run passes the throwaway key's path and password on the gradlew command line, so its random throwaway password is briefly visible in the process list, which the reviewer asked to avoid.

Why a: A value given explicitly for one build should beat a persistent default; it keeps the real key out of every test build and passwords off the command line, and your normal release setup behaves exactly as before.
